definition: Seminal means original and important; creating a field.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word seminal. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know seminal should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Choreographers still mine the 1972 kung-fu picture; its wire-work made it seminal for the whole genre.
Admired work wins the evening; it may still change nothing. Seminal work is still being answered decades later.
Influential work leaves a mark — later artists borrow a method here, an idea there; seminal goes further, naming the seed the whole field grew from.

Groundbreaking honors the first: nobody had managed the thing before, and the word asks nothing about what came after — a groundbreaking feat can stand alone forever. Seminal makes the further claim that later work grew from yours. Every seminal work broke ground somewhere; most groundbreaking feats never become seminal.

Foundational describes what a later structure visibly stands on — pull it out and the floors above sag. It looks from the finished building back down at its base. Seminal looks from the seed forward: the original work a field then grew from. A textbook can be foundational; the paper that started the field is seminal.

In 1978 a Florida teenager popped his skateboard off flat ground — no ramp, no hands — and landed with the board still under his feet.
Every kickflip, every stair trick, every contest run since descends from that one motion.
Skaters call the ollie seminal and mean it root and all: the seed the whole modern vocabulary grew from.
Seminal makes a claim fame can't: descent.
Plenty of famous tricks were dead ends — admired, replayed, never built upon.
The root is semin-, seed: a seminal work is one later work grows from.
If nothing grew from it, it may be brilliant, but it isn't seminal.
Seminal is the historian's word, awarded with hindsight: from this seed, the field.
Groundbreaking (its own synonym chip) honors a first; seminal requires descendants — call nothing seminal until you can name what grew from it.
Reserve it for the founding paper, album, or design, not merely the best one.

In 1866 Gregor Mendel published a quiet paper on pea plants, counting the ratios in which traits passed from one generation to the next.
Almost nobody read it; the journal sat unopened in libraries for thirty-four years, and Mendel died a monastery abbot, not a famous scientist.
Rediscovered in 1900, the paper proved seminal: the entire science of genetics grew out of its ratios.
Every later idea in the field — genes, chromosomes, inherited disease, crop breeding — traces its ancestry to those pea counts.
